sentences.text: The ground station estate is treated as a shared mission resource under the same configuration control principles that apply to command, telemetry, and processing services.
North S-Band Antenna provides the nominal early-pass command uplink and low-rate telemetry return for contacts that require conservative link margins.
South S-Band Antenna provides the alternate S-band path and is kept in a compatible configuration so that short-notice reassignment can be made without changing spacecraft procedures.
Kiruna X-Band Antenna is assigned primarily to high-rate payload downlink during European visibility periods and is planned with margin for setup, carrier acquisition, and post-contact checks.
Svalbard X-Band Antenna extends northern contact opportunities and is favored when the orbit geometry gives longer visibility or lower elevation loss.
The Mission Control Center maintains the operational contact schedule and uses it as the controlling reference for console staffing, command readiness, and telemetry coverage.
The Network Control System distributes station allocations, confirms antenna readiness states, and records the actual start and end times of each contact.
Contact booking requests are submitted through the Mission Planning System with the required service type, antenna preference, minimum elevation, data volume expectation, and priority class.
Routine contacts are frozen at the daily planning cut-off, while contingency contacts may be inserted later when approved operational justification is recorded.
Conflicts are resolved first by spacecraft safety need, then by data timeliness need, then by efficient use of common ground resources.
The Ground Network Manager is also known as Juniper in standing operational rosters.
The Ground Network Manager arbitrates unresolved contact conflicts and verifies that station commitments remain consistent with maintenance windows and staffing limits.
The Flight Dynamics Facility is also known as Mistral in legacy shift logs.
Flight Dynamics Facility provides visibility predictions and antenna pointing support products to the planning process before contacts are released for execution.
Orbit Determination Engine produces the Doppler Residual Report after each qualified tracking pass to support navigation trend assessment.
Local station teams are responsible for antenna pre-pass configuration, frequency standard verification, time correlation checks, safety interlocks, and logging of any local anomalies.

Station operators notify the Mission Control Center when local constraints could affect an approved contact, including equipment warm-up limits, access restrictions, or unexpected maintenance activity.
Ground Network Manager issues the Antenna Deicing Notice when forecast icing or measured buildup threatens tracking performance.
Weather constraints are assessed using local forecasts and real-time measurements for wind, precipitation, temperature, lightning risk, and atmospheric attenuation.
X-band contacts may be downgraded or moved when heavy precipitation is expected to reduce the link margin below the approved operating threshold.
S-band contacts are normally more tolerant of weather, but high winds or unsafe outdoor conditions can still make an antenna unavailable for service.
The Telemetry Ingest Service receives contact status and data-flow indicators so that downstream processing can distinguish planned gaps from station-side interruptions.
The Payload Processing Facility coordinates with Primary Processing Cluster and Backup Processing Cluster when a downlink allocation change alters expected processing load or delivery timing.
Ground network management practices emphasize advance coordination, disciplined change approval, continuous monitoring during contacts, and post-contact reconciliation against the approved schedule.
Performance trends for each antenna are reviewed at regular operations meetings so that recurring acquisition delays, pointing errors, or link-margin shortfalls are converted into corrective actions.
